summaries.example: Imagine a story about a round square. No real round square can be found, but you can still think about one and describe what would make it round and square. Meinong used examples like this to ask whether thinking always needs a real thing outside the mind.
summaries.summary: Alexius Meinong was a philosopher and psychologist who studied how minds think about things. He became famous for his theory of objects. He argued that thought is not limited to things that exist. We can think about a golden mountain, a unicorn, or even a round square. These objects may not exist, and some may be impossible, but they can still be discussed and described. Meinong also distinguished three parts of an experience: the mental act, its mental content, and the object it is about. For example, hoping for universal peace involves an act of hope and a mental content, even if universal peace has not happened. His theory of knowledge emphasized evidence, while allowing that some evidence supports only a reasonable guess rather than certainty. His early theory of value connected value with people’s feelings. Later, he argued that some values can be objective and that feelings help us recognize them. Bertrand Russell objected that Meinong’s view could create logical problems, especially when impossible objects were described. The disagreement helped make Meinong well known and encouraged later philosophers to develop new theories of logic and meaning.
key_ideas: Alexius Meinong was an Austrian philosopher and psychologist who worked mainly at the University of Graz.
He founded Austria-Hungary’s first psychological laboratory and also established a philosophical seminar.
His theory of objects included ordinary things, ideas, facts, impossible things, and things that do not exist.
He separated a mental experience from the object that the experience is about.
His views influenced discussions of language, logic, knowledge, mind, values, and emotions.
Bertrand Russell criticized Meinong’s theory, and that debate helped inspire later Meinongian approaches to logic and meaning.
summaries.why_it_matters: Meinong’s work asks a lasting question: how can language and thought be about things that are imaginary, missing, or impossible? His ideas help us notice the difference between thinking about something and that thing actually existing. They also show how philosophy can connect psychology, language, logic, knowledge, and values. Even when philosophers reject part of his theory, they may still learn from the problems he brought into view.

important_terms.definition: The study of what kinds of things there are, including real things and, in Meinong’s view, things that do not exist.
A mental experience aimed at something, such as seeing a tree, hoping for peace, or thinking about a unicorn.
A thing that can be thought about, judged, imagined, desired, or felt. Meinong included both existing and non-existing objects.
A thing’s features or way of being, considered separately from whether the thing exists.

questions_to_think_about: Can you think about something that does not exist?
Is imagining a thing the same as creating it?
When you feel that something is good, is the value only in your feeling?
Should every sentence that sounds like it names something have a real object behind it?

summaries.example: Consider the sentence, “Meinong believed that the round square is round.” Russell’s theory of descriptions treats “the round square” without assuming that such a thing exists. Meinong instead distinguishes the object’s characterized features from its mode of being: the object can be characterized as round and square without thereby existing. The dispute concerns whether ordinary grammar reveals logical form and how thought can refer to non-existent objects.
summaries.summary:
Alexius Meinong was an Austrian philosopher and psychologist whose work ranged across ontology, metaphysics, epistemology, philosophical psychology, logic, language, and value theory. He worked at the University of Graz, founded a psychological laboratory in 1894, and developed the theory of objects as the central discipline of a philosophical system. Unlike a metaphysics restricted to what is actual, Meinong’s theory of objects considers whatever can be an object of thought or experience. This includes existing real objects, ideal objects that merely subsist, incomplete objects, non-existent objects, and impossible objects.

A central distinction in Meinong’s psychology separates the act of an experience, its psychological content, and its object. The act and content exist as mental components, but the object may not exist. Meinong also distinguished psychological content from logical or conceptual content, and described consciousness through self-presentation: experiences can be apprehended directly without requiring a second mental representation of themselves. His classification of experiences included representations, judgments, feelings, and desires, with corresponding objects such as objecta, objectives, dignitatives, and desideratives. Assumptions entertain objectives without belief and therefore support imagination, questioning, reasoning, and artistic activity.

Meinong’s object theory relies on the independence of an object’s so-being from its being. Thus an object can be characterized in a certain way even if it does not exist. His account also distinguishes complete from incomplete objects and introduces nuclear and extra-nuclear determinations to separate ordinary properties from properties concerning an object’s status. key_ideas: Meinong treated philosophy as a group of interconnected sciences centered on mental phenomena, with psychology and the theory of objects playing fundamental roles.
His theory of objects extends ontology beyond existing things to include subsistent ideal objects, non-existent objects, incomplete objects, and impossible objects.
A mental experience has an act, a psychological content, and an object; the object need not exist, while the act and content are mental realities.
He distinguished serious experiences, such as perception and judgment, from fantasy experiences and assumptions, which entertain possibilities without conviction.
His epistemology combined evidence with fallibilism: knowledge requires entitlement and evidence, but critical examination can remain possible.

Russell argued that Meinong’s account generated contradictions and that descriptions should not be treated as names of objects; later Meinongian theories responded with distinctions in properties, predication, or logic.
summaries.why_it_matters: Meinong’s philosophy matters because it makes explicit several distinctions that remain important in analytic philosophy: existence versus predication, reference versus description, mental content versus object, and truth versus evidence. His treatment of non-existent and impossible objects challenged the assumption that meaningful thought must always correspond to an existing entity. Russell’s criticism exposed serious logical difficulties, but the controversy also encouraged later work in semantics, free logic, fictional reference, and non-classical logic. important_terms.definition: Meinong’s systematic study of objects as such, including what can be known about them independently of whether they exist.
The doctrine that an object’s properties, or so-being, are not determined by whether the object has being.
The view that an object is not itself committed to being or non-being, although a corresponding fact of being or non-being may hold.
A distinction between an object’s ordinary characterizing properties and properties concerning its status, such as being thought about or being complete.
An ideal object that is founded on other objects, such as a square formed by four nuts or a melody formed from notes.
A mental experience directed toward an object; Meinong analyzes it into an act, psychological content, and object.
Meinong’s later view that some values are not created by valuing subjects, though value experiences can disclose them.
A type of logic designed to contain some inconsistencies without allowing every statement to follow from them; later philosophers used it in Meinongian theories.

Can a theory consistently distinguish “being characterized as existent” from actually existing?
Are incomplete objects useful for explaining how language refers to fully determinate things?
Should impossible objects be governed by classical logical principles?
Did Meinong’s shift from value subjectivism to value objectivism solve the problems of his earlier view, or create new ones?

summaries.example: Suppose your class is planning a game about a “square circle.” Everyone knows that no ordinary object can really be both square and circular. Still, you can understand the words, imagine the idea, and discuss what follows from it. Meinong would say that thinking about this impossible object is not simply thinking about nothing. Russell would ask whether the sentence has been analyzed correctly before we accept that conclusion.
summaries.summary:
Alexius Meinong was an Austrian philosopher and psychologist who taught at the University of Graz. He founded a psychological laboratory and a philosophical seminar there. His work covered many subjects, but he is best known for the theory of objects. This theory asks what can be thought about, not only what exists. Meinong believed that the objects of thought can include ordinary things, ideal objects, missing things, fictional things, incomplete things, and impossible things. A round square cannot exist, but it can still be described and discussed.

Meinong’s account of the mind separates an experience into an act, a psychological content, and an object. If someone hopes for universal peace, the hoping and its mental content are real experiences, even if universal peace is not yet real. He also described self-presentation: we can sometimes notice our own experiences directly, without making a separate mental picture of them. His theory distinguishes serious experiences, such as perception and judgment, from fantasy experiences. Assumptions are especially important because they let us consider an idea without believing it. We use assumptions when asking questions, playing games, imagining stories, or reasoning about alternatives.

Meinong’s theory of knowledge made evidence central but allowed that some evidence supports only a presumption rather than certainty. He also developed a theory of meaning in which words express mental experiences and, through them, present objects. Incomplete objects can work as guides to more fully determined target objects. For example, “a brown square thing” may help someone think of a particular brown square without listing every property it has.

key_ideas: Meinong connected philosophy with psychology and believed philosophy should investigate experience carefully rather than simply present finished doctrines.
His theory of objects was broader than a theory limited to existing things.
He argued that an object’s described features can be considered independently of whether the object exists.
He distinguished judging from assuming: judgment involves conviction, while assumption allows us to explore an idea without believing it.
Meinong’s account of meaning linked words with mental experiences and with the objects presented through those experiences.
His early value theory emphasized value-feelings; his later theory treated some values as objective.
summaries.why_it_matters: Meinong’s ideas help explain why language and thought can concern absent, fictional, or impossible things. They also show why philosophers distinguish existence from description: saying that an object is round is not automatically the same as saying that it exists. His disagreements with Bertrand Russell became important for later discussions of logic, reference, meaning, and fictional objects. His work on assumptions and value-feelings also connects abstract philosophy with everyday activities such as imagining, judging, caring, and choosing.

important_terms.definition: The branch of philosophy that studies what exists and what kinds of things can be objects of thought.
The features an object is described as having, considered separately from whether it exists.
A thing that can be the target of a mental act, including something real, imaginary, incomplete, or impossible.
A mental act that is directed toward something, such as judging, imagining, feeling, or wanting.
A thought that entertains a possibility without claiming that it is true.
An object that is built upon or depends on other objects, such as a pattern formed by several separate items.
The view that values are not made entirely by people’s feelings, even though feelings can help us recognize values.

questions_to_think_about: When you imagine a fictional character, are you thinking about something or about nothing?
Why might a philosopher separate a word’s meaning from the thing it refers to?
Can an assumption be useful even when it is false?
Do people discover values, create them, or do both ideas apply in different ways?
